messages.content:
Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

Below is a high‑level “recipe” you could follow if you had two generic tools at your disposal: | Step | What to do | Why it matters | Tool you’d use | |------|------------|----------------|----------------| | **1. Gather context** | Ask the user for the missing pieces that a real ordering API would need:
• Location (address or ZIP code)
• Pickup vs. delivery
• Payment method (card, wallet, etc.)
• Any special instructions | APIs usually require these as query or body parameters. | Prompt the user (no tool needed) | | **2. Search for an ordering API** | Use the “search‑internet‑for‑API‑calls” tool to look for:
• McDonald’s official ordering API (rarely public)
• Third‑party delivery APIs that support McDonald’s (DoorDash, UberEats, Grubhub, etc.)
• Open‑source libraries or SDKs that wrap those services | You need a concrete endpoint to hit. | `search_internet_for_api_calls` | | **3. Inspect the API spec** | Once you have a candidate endpoint, fetch its OpenAPI/Swagger spec or read the documentation. Identify:
• Base URL
• Authentication scheme (OAuth2, API key, JWT, etc.)
• Required headers
• Request body schema (menu item IDs, quantities, modifiers)
• Response format | Knowing the contract lets you build a valid request. | `search_internet_for_api_calls` (or a manual fetch) | | **4. Authenticate** | If the API requires a token, perform the OAuth2 or API‑key exchange. Store the token for subsequent calls. | Without a valid token you’ll get 401/403 errors. | `execute_api_call` (POST to auth endpoint) | | **5. Build the order payload** | Using the spec, construct a JSON body that represents “Burger + Fries”. Example:
```json\n{\n \"location\": \"123 Main St, Springfield\",\n \"delivery\": false,\n \"items\": [\n {\"product_id\": \"BURGER_001\", \"quantity\": 1},\n {\"product_id\": \"FRIES_001\", \"quantity\": 1}\n ],\n \"payment_method\": \"card_visa_1234\"\n}\n``` | The payload must match the API’s schema. | Manual construction (no tool) | | **6. Place the order** | Send a POST request to the “create order” endpoint with the payload and the auth token in the header. | This is the actual “order” action. | `execute_api_call` (POST) | | **7. Handle the response** | Parse the JSON response:
• Order ID
• Estimated ETA
• Status (“confirmed”, “queued”, etc.)
• Error messages if any | Gives the user confirmation or lets you retry. | `execute_api_call` (response parsing) | | **8. Poll for status (optional)** | If the API supports it, periodically GET `/orders/{id}/status` until the order is “delivered” or “completed”. | Keeps the user informed. | `execute_api_call` (GET) | | **9. Notify the user** | Send a friendly message: “Your Burger & Fries are on their way! Order #12345, ETA 25 min.” | Completes the user experience. | No tool needed | ### Quick pseudo‑code sketch ```python # 1. Get user context location = "123 Main St, Springfield" delivery = False payment_token = "tok_visa_1234" # 2. Search for API api_info = search_internet_for_api_calls(query="McDonald's ordering API") base_url = api_info["base_url"] # e.g. https://api.doordash.com/v1 auth_endpoint = api_info["auth_endpoint"] # 3. Authenticate auth_resp = execute_api_call( url=auth_endpoint, method="POST", headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}, body={"client_id": "...", "client_secret": "...", "grant_type": "client_credentials"} ) access_token = auth_resp["access_token"] # 4. Build order payload order_payload = { "location": location, "delivery": delivery, "items": [ {"product_id": "BURGER_001", "quantity": 1}, {"product_id": "FRIES_001", "quantity": 1} ], "payment_method": payment_token } # 5. Place order order_resp = execute_api_call( url=f"{base_url}/orders", method="POST", headers={ "Authorization": f"Bearer {access_token}", "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body=order_payload ) # 6. Check result if order_resp["status"] == "confirmed": print(f"Order placed! ID: {order_resp['order_id']}") else: print(f"Failed to place order: {order_resp['error']}") ``` ### Things to watch out for | Issue | Mitigation | |-------|------------| | **No public McDonald’s API** | Fall back to a delivery partner API (DoorDash, UberEats, etc.). | | **Location mismatch** | Verify the address is serviceable by the chosen partner. | | **Payment failures** | Validate card/token before sending the order. | | **Rate limits / throttling** | Respect `Retry-After` headers; implement exponential back‑off. | | **Privacy** | Never log sensitive payment data; use secure storage for tokens. | With this workflow you can systematically turn “order a burger and fries” into a series of concrete API calls, leveraging the two tools you described.
